Comparing river gauges

1 Introduction

A river gauge records the water level at a fixed point. Two gauges along the same river can record different heights because the bed changes as the river flows through a valley. We compare daily readings over a full season.

Before comparing the gauges, we check their positions against a common reference. Each station records height above its own marker. The markers sit at different elevations, so equal readings do not tell us whether both stations saw the same water level.

We compare changes over time at each site. A sharp rise should appear first at the upstream station, then at the downstream one. That timing gives a second way to check which peaks belong to the same storm.

We keep the original readings for every station so that the comparison can be repeated with a different baseline. Stations that were moved during the season need a separate baseline for each period. The dates of those moves are recorded beside the readings.

1.1 Related Work

Earlier surveys compared gauges by following the same storms. Matching each peak to the time of rainfall helped separate changes in the river from errors in the gauges.

1.2 Daily readings

We use the start of each day as the reference time and subtract the first reading from the rest. The final plot shows the change at each station over the season.
